name: Standardised weapon production in Qin state workshops
summary: Qin workshops made tens of thousands of near-identical bronze weapons in supervised cells, to shared models and moulds, with inscriptions naming those responsible.
description: Study of the roughly 40,000 bronze weapons buried with the Terracotta Army shows they were made in multi-skilled cells under centralised supervision, with defined models, moulds and quality-control procedures. Long inscriptions on lances and halberds give the regnal year, the person in charge, the workshop and the individual worker. The weapons belong to the First Emperor's mausoleum, built between 246 and 210 BC; where the workshops stood is not known.

impact.note: A state workshop system serving one society's armies (reach 1) that made uniform goods in vast numbers with accountable makers, a new organisational capability (depth 2), with Han state workshops as its known successors (generativity 1); reach lowered from the lead's 2 because no wider descent is evidenced.

events.statement: The bronze weapons made for the Terracotta Army were produced in multi-skilled cells under centralised supervision, with defined models, moulds and quality-control procedures; the date is the mausoleum's building span given in the first event.

evidence.supports: production was organised in multi-skilled cells that worked under centralised supervision, with well-defined models, moulds and quality-control procedures

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Do the Houma foundry or Shang piece-mould casting have a stronger claim to be the first standardised production?
How close do the crossbow triggers come to interchangeable parts? The sources read do not measure this.
The companion paper on inscriptions and finishing marks (Journal of Archaeological Science, 2011) was not read.
The second event takes its dates from the first event's quotation; the paper gives no closer date for the weapons, though it says their long inscriptions carry regnal years.
The place is the findspot; the workshops' location is unknown.

research.note: The sources read do not address priority or whether Qin workshops drew on earlier workshops, so origin is unknown.
